# Finite halfspace volumes can uniquely force a nonpolytope

This is an obstruction to a general exact finite-cap polytope-replacement
theorem. It is entirely continuous, in dimension four. It says nothing
against replacement for special low-depth cap certificates or against OC.

## 1. The body and finite measurements

Use coordinates (x_1,x_2,t,s) in R^4. Let B be the unit disk in R^2 and

    C=B times [0,3] times [0,3].

This is a convex body of volume 9pi and is not a polytope. Put epsilon=1/10.
The following twenty-two closed halfspaces, together with total volume,
uniquely determine C among all convex bodies:

1. The eight exterior halfspaces x_i>=1, x_i<=-1 (i=1,2), t<=0,
   t>=3, s<=0, s>=3, each of whose intersections with C has volume zero.
2. The four halfspaces t<=1, t<=2, s<=1, s<=2, whose volumes are,
   respectively, 3pi,6pi,3pi,6pi.
3. For i=1,2 and j=0,1, the eight halfspaces

       t>=j+1/2+epsilon x_i,
       s>=j+1/2+epsilon x_i.

   Each has volume 3pi(5/2-j).
4. The two halfspaces t+s<=1/2+epsilon x_i, i=1,2, each of whose
   volumes is 101pi/800.

The theorem below proves uniqueness. Hence no polytope can have these
same cap volumes and total volume. Total volume may also be encoded by
one additional containing halfspace, for example t<=4, once the zero
exterior-cap constraints are retained.

## 2. Three equal slab volumes force a prism

**Lemma 1.** Let L be a convex body in R^(r+1), with coordinates (y,t),
contained in 0<=t<=3. If its three closed unit slabs

    L_i=L intersect {i<=t<=i+1}, i=0,1,2,

all have the same positive (r+1)-volume, then for a convex body K in R^r
and a vector v in R^r,

    L={(y+t v,t): y in K, 0<=t<=3}.                       (2)

**Proof.** Convexity gives (L_0+L_2)/2 subset L_1. Ordinary Brunn--Minkowski
gives volume at least the common slab volume. It equals that volume by
containment. The equality case of ordinary Brunn--Minkowski for positive
full-dimensional convex bodies says L_0 and L_2 are homothetic; their
equal volumes make them translates. Also the contained midpoint body
equals L_1, since both are full-dimensional compact convex sets of the
same volume. Thus L_2=L_0+q and L_1=L_0+q/2.

Let the full t-projection of L be [alpha,beta]. Positive volume of the
outer slabs gives alpha<1 and beta>2. Its sections at t=1 and t=2 are
full-dimensional within those planes: interior points exist on both sides,
and their joining segment passes through the interior of L. Therefore
the projections of L_0,L_1,L_2 are [alpha,1],[1,2],[2,beta].

Translation gives q_t=2-alpha and beta=3-alpha. The midpoint body's
projection is [1+alpha/2,2-alpha/2], which must equal [1,2]. Hence
alpha=0, beta=3, and q_t=2. Write q=(2v,2).

Let K_t be the y-section at level t. The translate relations give
K_(t+1)=K_t+v for 0<=t<=2. For any linear functional u, the support
function h(t)=h_(K_t)(u) is concave in t, because convexity gives the
corresponding Minkowski inclusions of sections. Put f(t)=h(t)-t u dot v.
Then f is concave and f(t+1)=f(t).

For 0<=r<=1, concavity between 0 and 1 gives f(r)>=f(0). Concavity at
1 as a combination of 0 and r+1 gives

    f(0)=f(1)>=[r f(0)+f(r+1)]/(r+1),

so f(r)<=f(0). Thus f is constant on [0,3]. Every section has the
support function of K_0+t v, proving (2). Positive volume then makes
K_0 a full-dimensional body. QED.

The only equality theorem used here is the standard continuous
Brunn--Minkowski equality characterization, not a mixed-integer result.

## 3. Two slab rigidities force a double prism

Let L be any convex body with the measurements of Section 1. A zero-volume
exterior cap forces containment in its complementary closed halfspace:
any point strictly outside, joined toward an interior point of a body,
would give a positive-volume exterior part. Thus

    L subset [-1,1]^2 times [0,3]^2.                      (3)

The total and four slab measurements make all three t-slabs and all three
s-slabs have volume 3pi. Lemma 1 applies in both coordinates.

The first prism structure implies that the (t,s)-projection is a
parallelogram of the form

    0<=t<=3,       alpha+a t<=s<=beta+a t,

with beta>alpha. The second prism structure implies its horizontal
sections have one fixed positive length for every s in its full interval
of projection, namely [0,3]. If a were nonzero, horizontal sections near
the minimum s of the displayed parallelogram would have lengths tending
to zero and varying strictly with s. This contradicts that constant
positive length. Hence a=0, and the projection is exactly [0,3]^2.
Similarly the s-prism translation has no t-component.

Writing the remaining translations in the x-coordinates as v,w in R^2,
the two structures combine to give

    L={(y+t v+s w,t,s): y in K, 0<=t,s<=3}                (4)

for a planar convex body K. For example, first translate the (t,s)-fiber
back along t to (0,s), then back along s to (0,0); the operations commute.
The triangular shear in (4) has determinant one, so |K|=pi.

Containment (3) gives |v_i|,|w_i|<=2/3 for each coordinate: fix y and
the other slab coordinate and compare its x_i-values at the two ends of
a length-three slab. Let m_i=|K|^(-1) integral_K y_i be the centroid.

## 4. Eight tilted-cap measurements remove all shear and translation

Consider the cap t>=j+1/2+epsilon x_i in the parametrization (4). Its
threshold is

    t >= [j+1/2+epsilon(y_i+s w_i)]/(1-epsilon v_i).       (5)

The denominator is positive since |v_i|<=2/3. The threshold lies between
j and j+1 for every y,s: at these two levels the original cap margin is
-1/2-epsilon x_i<0 and 1/2-epsilon x_i>0, respectively, by |x_i|<=1.
Thus no truncation of the affine threshold by 0 or 3 occurs in integration.

The cap volume is exactly

    3|K|[3-(j+1/2+epsilon(m_i+(3/2)w_i))/(1-epsilon v_i)]. (6)

Its prescribed value is 3pi(5/2-j). Using |K|=pi, equality becomes

    m_i+(3/2)w_i=-(j+1/2)v_i.                            (7)

The two values j=0,1 force v_i=0 and m_i+(3/2)w_i=0.
The s-caps give symmetrically w_i=0 and m_i+(3/2)v_i=0.
Consequently

    v=w=0,       centroid(K)=0,       L=K times [0,3]^2.  (8)

This calculation uses individual halfspace volumes, without requiring
measurements of halfspace intersections with auxiliary cells.

## 5. Two corner caps force the disk

For a fixed y in K, the cap t+s<=1/2+epsilon y_i cuts a triangle of area
(1/2)(1/2+epsilon y_i)^2 in the (t,s)-square. Its threshold lies between
2/5 and 3/5 by (3), so the triangle is entirely inside that square.
Using (8), its volume is

    |K|/8+(epsilon/2) integral_K y_i
          +(epsilon^2/2) integral_K y_i^2
      =pi/8+(epsilon^2/2) integral_K y_i^2.              (9)

For the unit disk, integral_B y_i^2=pi/4, as follows by polar coordinates.
Thus the prescribed volume 101pi/800 and epsilon=1/10 force

    integral_K y_1^2=integral_K y_2^2=pi/4,
    integral_K |y|^2=pi/2=integral_B |y|^2.              (10)

Among all measurable sets of area pi, the unit disk uniquely minimizes
this radial second moment up to null sets. The required elementary proof
is the identity, using |K|=|B|,

    integral_K |y|^2-integral_B |y|^2
      =integral_(K\B)(|y|^2-1)
         +integral_(B\K)(1-|y|^2) >=0.

Each integrand is strictly positive off the unit circle on its domain.
Equality therefore gives equality of K and B almost everywhere. Compact
convex bodies with interior that agree almost everywhere agree exactly:
a point strictly outside the other body creates a positive-volume
difference by joining toward an interior ball. Hence K=B and L=C.

## 6. Conclusion

The finite measurements of Section 1 uniquely force the nonpolytope C.
In particular no theorem can replace an arbitrary continuous convex body
by a polytope while preserving an arbitrary finite list of halfspace
volumes and total volume exactly. Preserving every arrangement-cell
volume is stronger and is also impossible here.

This obstruction does not contradict the planar replacement theorem in
`candidate 98181ddbde71e951`, nor does it rule out a
replacement tailored to low-depth active circuits. It closes the general
dimension-free replacement mechanism without that additional structure.

The rational coefficient computations in the shear and moment formulas
are checked in `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_finite_caps_force_nonpolytope.py`. The slab rigidity
and uniqueness proof are the exact geometric arguments above, not numerical
tests.
